power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "P ≥ 0.05", Text = "Crosses indicate correlations that were not statistically significant after adjustment for multiple testing (adjusted P ≥ 0.05)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p=7.49", "p=3.00", "p=3.73", "p=0.128", "p=0.15", "P ≥ 0.05"), Sentence = c("In exploratory analyses pooling vaccine groups, EBOV-and BDBV-reactive total cytokine-producing CD4⁺ T-cell responses were strongly correlated at both D14 (Spearman ρ=0.93, adjusted p=7.49×10⁻) and D70 (ρ=0.76, adjusted p=0.0024).", "Positive correlations were also observed for CD8⁺ Tcell responses at D14 (ρ=0.57, adjusted p=0.033) and D70 (ρ=0.88, adjusted p=3.00×10⁻); (Figure 3A).", "At Month 3, BDBV GP-binding antibody levels were positively correlated with binding to both EBOV Mayinga GP (ρ=0.71, adjusted p=3.73×10⁻) and EBOV Kikwit GP (ρ=0.46, adjusted p=0.014) (Figure 3B).", "In EVD survivors, EBOV-and BDBV-reactive CD4⁺ T-cell responses were positively correlated (Spearman ρ=0.81, adjusted p=0.029), whereas the corresponding CD8⁺ T-cell association did not reach statistical significance (ρ=0.65, adjusted p=0.128).", "Similarly, BDBV GP-binding antibody levels were positively correlated with binding to EBOV Mayinga GP (ρ=0.67, adjusted p=0.0496), whereas the association with EBOV Kikwit GP was not statistically significant (ρ=0.49, adjusted p=0.15) (Supplementary Figure 3).", "Crosses indicate correlations that were not statistically significant after adjustment for multiple testing (adjusted P ≥ 0.05)." )), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

summary_table.ethics_statements: Study protocols were approved by the relevant ethics committees in Guinea and France, including INSERM/CEEI and IRD/CCDE for Postebogui and INSERM IRB00003888 for PREVAC.
live_data_statements: Here, we analysed paired serum and peripheral blood mononuclear cell samples from healthy participants enrolled in the PREVAC vaccine trial 7 and Ebola virus disease (EVD) survivors from the Postebogui cohort 6 to characterize both humoral and cellular responses to EBOV, BDBV, SUDV and MARV.

Participants were selected from two previously described studies: the multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled phase II PREVAC vaccine trial (NCT02876328) and the Postebogui cohort of laboratory-confirmed EVD survivors, both conducted in Guinea [12] [13] [14] [15] [16].
From PREVAC, adult participants enrolled in Guinea were randomised to Ad26.
All participants provided written informed consent for sample collection, storage, and use.
